newsitem.title: UK: Mad cow nearly gone in young British herds.
newsitem.headline: Mad cow nearly gone in young British herds.

text.p: A selective nationwide slaughter has virtually eliminated mad cow disease from younger British cattle, scientists said on Tuesday.
But they said Europe should begin assessing the spread of scrapie, a similar disease in sheep, and should try to breed it out of sheep herds.
Roy Anderson, an epidemiologist at Oxford University, said the cull of British cattle infected with Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease) was working well.
"We believe it is possible to take the epidemic out by mid-1998," Anderson told a news conference.
The cull was introduced after the European Union imposed a worldwide ban on British beef exports.

Anderson said the current rate of 55,000 cattle aged over 30 months being slaughtered every week would have to be maintained. The British agriculture ministry said on Monday that nearly one million cattle had been killed in this effort to wipe out the BSE epidemic and restore confidence in British beef.
Anderson, speaking after a meeting of European scientists on mad cow disease and scrapie, added: "Perhaps as few as 150 animals are infected under 30 months of age."
BSE and its human form, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD), take a long time to incubate. Mutant proteins build up gradually, destroying the brain and killing the victim.
Britain has promised to destroy all older cattle, considered most at risk, and now removes potentially infected parts from all cattle slaughtered for food use.
Anderson cast doubt on a report published on Tuesday that predicted hundreds of Britons would die each year from eating BSE-infected beef.
The report, published in the Independent newspaper, cited a study by scientists at the CJD Surveillance Unit in Edinburgh.

"It looks as though the total number of cases over the whole course of the disease will be in hundreds, rather than thousands," said James Ironside, co-author of the paper to be published in the Lancet medical journal.

But Anderson said it was too early to make such a prediction. "My own view is that it is quite difficult to say anything sensible, scientifically, at this point," he said. "It will be a number of years...before we can say."
Fourteen people have died of a new type of CJD that scientists say probably came from eating infected beef.
The incubation period for the disease can range anywhere from five to 30 years and, as the BSE epidemic peaked in the 1980s, it will be years before some victims develop symptoms.
John Wilesmith of Britain's Central Veterinary Laboratory said scientists were also checking to see whether BSE somehow got back into sheep.
There is no evidence of this spread, but it is theoretically possible as sheep, cows and other animals are routinely fed the rendered remains of one another in feed meant to boost growth.
Scientists think cows got BSE from eating the rendered remains of sheep infected with scrapie.
Although there is no evidence people can get CJD from scrapie-infected sheep, some experts say all potentially infected parts should be removed just to be safe.
